about: logicbook14: the series' extra editions, built the same way as the books (tools/book/build_series.py, then BOOK_SERIES=1 build_pdfs.js, then build_epub.py and listing_kdp.py). pocket: "The Logic Behind It", a 5 x 8 in standard-colour paperback (72 to 80 pages, KDP's minimum for standard colour is 72) and a Kindle ebook, made from assets/js/logic-library.js (items, in this order, one per page; the words are the library's own) and tools/book/pocket.py (the pages around them). It is sold on Amazon only and is not in KDP Select. notes_pages tunes the page count. boxset: one Kindle ebook with Books 1 to 4 and the pocket guide, its own front cover (a JPG only: there is no print box set). isbn fields stay empty until the owner buys ISBNs.

pocket.title: The Logic Behind It
pocket.sub: A Pocket Guide to Why People React the Way They Do
pocket.line: Thirty-eight everyday reactions, one to a page, with the logic behind each one and a kind next step.
pocket.blurb: A friend leaves the party without a goodbye. A colleague’s feedback lands like a slap. Someone says “I’m fine” when they plainly aren’t. Most reactions that look odd, rude or over the top from outside have a logic behind them, and it makes sense once you can see it. This pocket guide lays that logic out for thirty-eight everyday situations, one to a page. Each page shows what the reaction looks like from outside, the reasoning step by step, an everyday picture that works the same way, the other person’s side, and one sentence and one small step that help you both. It runs both ways. Some pages explain neurodivergent logic, some explain common social habits like small talk and hints, and many cover things anyone does. Every page has a code to its free online version, and blank cards at the back help you work out your own.
pocket.overrides_about: Print and ebook wording only (the online library keeps its own): field, or field.N for one step of the chain or one analogy. They bring each page to at most one "X, not Y" and fewer colons, as the series style asks. "care" lines are never changed.

plan-changed.an.0: A sat nav recalculating while you’re already on the motorway. For a moment it has no route at all.
plan-changed.looks: Ten to seven. “Oh, change of plan, we’re meeting at the other place, and Jo’s coming!” Mel says “Great.” Then she says almost nothing for the next hour.
plan-changed.other: To the person who changed it, it was nothing much, maybe even a nice surprise. Now they feel their good idea has been treated like bad news.
chain: A plan is a map the mind has already walked
A late change means redrawing it, fast, with no warning
Redrawing burns the energy that was meant for the evening

late-again.an.0: A watch with only two settings, “plenty of time” and “too late”.
late-again.fits: For many people with ADHD, sensing time passing is genuinely harder. Researchers describe it as part of how attention and self-control work. It says nothing about how much someone cares.
late-again.say: “I misjudge time. You matter to me, and I’m working on it.”
late-again.step: Set the alarm for leaving, not arriving, and text “Leaving now” as you go. Whoever’s waiting can agree a time to start without you.
late-again.looks: Twenty past, and here they are at the door with their coat half on and a breathless apology, for the third time this month. They plainly care, and they are also plainly late.
late-again.other: Waiting tells the waiting person they matter less, whatever was meant. It costs them real time, sometimes a cold dinner or a missed film, and over months it wears down trust.
chain: Some minds have two settings for time, “now” and “not now”
“Not now” turns into “now” all at once, with no warning in between
Getting ready takes longer than the guess said it would
So they’re late, and they did care, both

coffee-sometime.an.0: A wave across the street. It means “hello, I see you”, not “come over”.
coffee-sometime.step: If you want it to happen, ask “Shall we pick a day?” If you said “sometime” and don’t mean it yet, don’t worry. The other person can ask too.
coffee-sometime.looks: “We should get coffee sometime!” Then nothing. No day, no text, for about five months.
coffee-sometime.other: If you take words at face value, you heard a plan. You waited. When nothing came, it felt like a small promise broken, and you may not have said so.
chain: It’s a friendly signal, not a booking
It means “I like you and I’m open to more”
A date would turn it into a promise neither of you has checked

maybe-means-no.an.0: A dimmer switch instead of a light switch. The light still goes off, just gently.
maybe-means-no.step: It’s fair to ask, kindly, “Is that a maybe-yes or a maybe-no?” And honestly, a clear “No, but thank you” is kinder than it sounds.
maybe-means-no.looks: “Maybe. I’ll see how I feel.” Everyone else at the table seems to know that means no. You’ve kept a seat.
maybe-means-no.other: For someone who takes words at face value, the question is still open. They keep a seat, wait for an answer, and later feel quietly misled.
chain: A flat “no” can feel like a door shut in someone’s face
“Maybe” lets the other person down slowly
Nobody gets refused out loud, so nobody loses face

left-party.fits: A long goodbye costs energy too, with a round of hugs and small talk at the door. For people who find social time draining, including many autistic people, the quiet exit still leaves them able to get home safely.
left-party.step: Send a short text afterwards, such as “Thanks for tonight, I had to go when my battery ran out.” Hosts can say up front, “Slip out whenever you need to.”
left-party.looks: You look round for Ross to say goodbye. Ross went forty minutes ago. There was, apparently, a wave from the door.
left-party.an.0: A phone on 3% that shuts everything down except the call you’re on.
left-party.other: The host is left wondering if something went wrong. Friends aren’t sure whether to text and ask, so mostly they don’t.
chain: Energy is a budget
The party spent it faster than expected
Staying past zero risks a shutdown, or a sharp word to someone who didn’t deserve it
Slipping out protects the evening and the friendship

headphones.an.0: Sunglasses on a bright day. You still see everything, just without squinting.
headphones.say: “These help me stay at the table. Tap my arm and I’m all yours.”
headphones.step: Agree a signal, a tap on the arm, that means “I’m talking to you”. Where you can, turn the room down for everyone. One conversation at a time is kinder to more people than you’d think.
headphones.looks: Sunday lunch, nine people, the telly on and two conversations going at once, and one person at the end of the table has earbuds in with nothing playing through them at all.
headphones.other: From across the table it looks like a closed door. Most people won’t knock on it, so they talk round the person instead, and the person notices.
chain: Sound arrives whether you want it or not
A brain that filters less hears all of it at once
Headphones do the filtering, so there’s attention left over for the people

cancel-tired.looks: Friday, 4.52pm. “So sorry, I can’t do tonight x”. The table’s booked for half seven.
cancel-tired.fits: Rest is what makes good company possible. Sometimes the kindest thing a tired person can offer is a better evening later.
cancel-tired.say: “I’m empty, not uninterested. Can we pick a new day now?”
cancel-tired.an.0: Pulling into the services when you’re too tired to drive safely.
cancel-tired.other: The friend may have cleared their evening, booked the table or simply been looking forward to it. A late cancel can feel like coming last.
chain: Energy comes back with rest
This week used all of it up
Going out on empty means turning up in body only
cancel-tired.step: Cancel as early as you can, and put a new date in the same message. If it keeps happening, make the plans lighter, a walk, say, or a takeaway on the sofa where nobody has to put proper shoes on.

blunt.looks: You asked what she thought of your draft. She tells you. “The second half doesn’t work.” Full stop.
blunt.fits: For many autistic people, saying what they mean plainly is the honest, respectful option. Research on the “double empathy problem” suggests mix-ups between differently wired people run both ways, so the plain speaker isn’t the only one missing signals.
blunt.step: Add one warm line before the fact, such as “There’s a lot here I like.” The listener can ask for it too. “Start with one thing that works, then tell me straight.”
blunt.other: Words land on feelings as well as facts. If you spent a fortnight on that second half, “it doesn’t work” can sound a lot like “you don’t work”.
chain: The aim is to help the work be right
Soft words can bury the point
A clear point is quicker to fix
Saying it straight is a way of respecting your time

im-fine.an.0: A “Back in 10 minutes” sign on a shop door.
im-fine.looks: A rough day is written all over his face, and every question gets the same two words. “I’m fine.”
im-fine.other: People who take words at face value believe it, then get blamed for not noticing. Others feel shut out, or keep asking and seem nosy.
chain: Some feelings are too big to open in passing
“Fine” politely closes the lid for now
It protects the queue, the meeting, the school run
Often it means “not here, not now”, and leaves later open
im-fine.step: Try swapping “fine” for “Not now. Later tonight?” And if you’re the one asking, “Now or later?” goes down better than “What’s wrong?”

hints.fits: Researchers who study indirect speech argue that hints let people make requests while leaving everyone room to decline without embarrassment. It is a way of being polite.
hints.other: Hints get missed by lots of people, autistic or not. Then the hinter feels ignored, and somebody gets blamed for not doing a thing nobody actually asked for.
hints.step: Add the ask to the hint. “It’s cold. Could you close the window?” The listener can check, “Would you like me to close it?”
hints.looks: “Bit chilly in here, isn’t it?” Half an hour later Pat is quietly fuming because nobody shut the window.
chain: A straight request can sound like an order
A hint offers the idea without any pressure
The other person can take it up as if it were their own idea, or not

teasing.an.0: Puppies play-fighting. The teeth never close.
teasing.step: Check now and then. “Was that okay?” Agree what’s off limits, and drop any joke that keeps landing as hurt, however good you think it is.
teasing.looks: Two old friends calling each other terrible names across a pub table, both of them looking thoroughly delighted.
teasing.other: Someone who takes words literally, or who was teased cruelly at school, may hear only the insult. It stings, and they may not feel able to say so.
chain: Teasing says “we’re close enough to joke”
The insult works because both know it isn’t true
Laughing together proves the closeness, again

no-eye-contact.step: Check understanding with words instead of eyes, with the listener summing up one line of what they heard. Hard talks can happen side by side, on a walk or in the car.
no-eye-contact.looks: While you’re talking, he looks at the table, or out of the window, or at his own hands, anywhere really except at you.
no-eye-contact.other: Most of us were taught that eye contact means “I’m with you”. Without it, it’s very easy to feel ignored, or think they’re bored, or hiding something.
chain: Eyes carry a huge amount of information
Reading a face and following words at the same time splits attention
Looking away frees attention for the words
So looking away can be how he listens harder

small-talk.an.0: Musicians tuning up before the concert. There’s no tune yet, but it makes the tune possible.
small-talk.looks: “Turned cold again.” “Hasn’t it.” “Roadworks on the high street still.” “I know.” Five minutes of this, between two people who barely know each other.
small-talk.other: If you find it pointless or tiring, and many autistic people do, it costs energy and gives back no new information. Why is everyone so interested in rain?
chain: Strangers need a safe way to check each other out
The weather has no risk in it at all
Swapping easy lines says “I’m friendly, you can relax”
Once both feel safe, real talk can start
small-talk.step: Keep two easy lines ready, and one real question (“What’s keeping you busy at the moment?”). It’s fine to steer towards something you care about after a minute or so.

white-lie.step: Find something true and kind to say, like “You remembered I like blue. Thank you.” Honest people can use this too, and nobody has to lie.
white-lie.looks: A jumper in a shade of orange nobody has ever worn on purpose. “Oh, I love it!”
white-lie.an.0: Praising a five-year-old’s drawing of you that is mostly a triangle.
white-lie.other: If you value plain honesty, and many autistic people do, it simply feels like a lie. And then you start wondering what else isn’t true.
chain: The present is a message, and the message is “I thought of you”
The truth about the jumper would answer the wrong message
“I love it” answers the care, not the wool

how-are-you.step: Answer the ritual with the ritual. “Good, thanks, you?” Save the real answer for people who stop, sit down or ask twice.
how-are-you.looks: “All right? How are you?” says a colleague, who is still walking, and is already most of the way down the corridor.
how-are-you.an.0: A nod across a busy room.
how-are-you.other: A literal listener answers properly, with the hospital appointment and everything, and is left talking to the back of someone’s head. For anyone going through something hard, the ritual can feel very lonely.
chain: It’s a greeting that happens to be shaped like a question
Its job is to say “hello, I see you”
A short answer finishes the greeting

mask-crash.fits: Research with autistic adults describes “camouflaging”, working hard to appear like everyone else, often followed by exhaustion. Long stretches of it are linked with autistic burnout. Children and adults who aren’t autistic can do a version of this too.
mask-crash.looks: Her teachers say she’s an absolute delight. At ten past four she slams the front door, and at twenty past she falls apart over being given the wrong cup.
mask-crash.an.0: Swimming a length underwater and gasping at the far end.
mask-crash.other: The family gets the hardest hour of the day, every day, which feels unfair and baffling, especially when school sees none of it.
chain: Fitting in all day takes effort that doesn’t show
The effort is held in until it’s safe to stop
Home feels safe, so it lets go there
The crash is a sign home is trusted

written-please.say: “I ask for it in writing so I get it right first time. I trust what we agreed.”
written-please.step: After a chat, send a two-line summary. “So I’m doing X by Friday. Right?” The manager only has to reply “Yes.”
written-please.looks: Ten-minute briefing, lots of nodding. At the end: “Sorry, could you just pop that in an email?”
written-please.other: The manager may hear “I don’t trust what you said”, or just one more job at five o’clock.
chain: Spoken words vanish as they’re said
Holding them while you work splits your attention
Written steps can be checked again, and again

last-minute.fits: For many people with ADHD, getting started depends on interest, novelty or urgency more than importance. Researchers link this to how motivation and self-control work in ADHD. It has nothing to do with laziness.
last-minute.looks: The report had a month. It gets written between ten at night and two in the morning, with crisps.
last-minute.an.0: An old car that only starts on a downhill.
last-minute.other: Colleagues or family carry the stress of not knowing whether it’ll be done, and sometimes end up quietly covering for it at nine the next morning.
chain: Interest and urgency switch the engine on
A deadline weeks away doesn’t
When the deadline finally arrives, the engine starts
Late work is usually a starting problem, and the caring was there all along

disagree-later.say: “I raised it afterwards so it would be heard. I wasn’t going behind anyone’s back.”
disagree-later.step: Teams can offer both routes. “Say it now, or message me after.” Quiet disagreers can say “I’ve a different view, I’ll send it after.”
disagree-later.looks: Nods all the way through the meeting. Then, by the lifts, quietly: “Between you and me, I don’t think it’ll work.”
disagree-later.other: If you value saying things openly, it can look two-faced, and the meeting itself starts to feel like a bit of a performance.
chain: Disagreeing in public can make people dig in
A quiet word later lets them change their mind without losing face
So the point gets through more often

feedback-sandwich.step: Ask straight out, “What’s the one thing I should change?” If you’re giving it, say the fix clearly first, then one true good thing.
feedback-sandwich.looks: “Great energy! The whole report needs rewriting. Lovely formatting, though!”
feedback-sandwich.an.0: Hiding a tablet in a dog’s dinner.
feedback-sandwich.other: A literal listener may miss the middle entirely, or learn to distrust praise because it always seems to come before bad news.
chain: Criticism on its own makes people defensive
Praise round it keeps ears open
Open ears take in the fix

love-in-deeds.step: Agree one word and one deed. The doer says “I love you” on the way out, and the talker notices the deeds out loud.
love-in-deeds.looks: Stan hardly ever says “I love you”. He does fix the bike, fill the car and make the packed lunches at ten to seven every morning.
love-in-deeds.other: If you hear love mainly in words, you can feel unloved while surrounded by kind acts, which is a strange and lonely place to be.
chain: Love can be said or done
For some people, doing feels truer than saying
Fixing the bike is the message

quiet-in-fight.step: Say a return time. “I need twenty minutes. I’ll come back at eight.” Then come back at eight.
quiet-in-fight.looks: Halfway through the row he stops answering and looks at the floor, and somehow his saying nothing at all makes it worse.
quiet-in-fight.other: Silence can feel like being shut out, or punished. If you’re someone who needs to settle things before you can calm down, it can be frightening.
chain: A fast argument floods the body
A flooded brain can’t find good words
Silence stops the bad ones getting out
Going quiet is braking, not punishment

reassurance.step: Agree a kind limit together. One clear answer, then “I said it, and I meant it,” and something calming to do side by side.
reassurance.looks: “Are you sure you’re not cross with me?” It’s the fourth time tonight, and you give the same answer you gave the other three times, a bit more tightly.
reassurance.an.0: Going back for the third time to check the front door is locked.
reassurance.other: Answering the same question for the fourth time is tiring, and it can start to feel like your word isn’t trusted. Answering it again and again can also keep the loop going, which is the unkind part of an act of kindness.
chain: Doubt feels like danger
Reassurance switches the alarm off for a moment
The alarm comes back on
Asking again is trying to switch it off again

you-should-know.step: Agree that saying it out loud is allowed and still counts as being loved. The guesser can ask, “I can see something’s up. Tell me?”
you-should-know.looks: Something is very clearly wrong. She won’t say what. What seems to hurt most is that he hasn’t guessed.
you-should-know.other: For a lot of people, autistic or not, mind-reading just isn’t available. The guesser feels tested, and set up to fail the test.
chain: Being understood without asking feels like proof of love
Having to explain feels like it spoils the proof
So the hint stays a hint
It’s a hope, and nobody meant it as a trap

meltdown.fits: Autistic young people describe meltdowns as different from tantrums. They come from overload rather than from wanting something, and they are not chosen. Children and adults can both have them.
meltdown.step: During one: fewer words, less noise, more space, and safety first. Afterwards, rest. The calm talk about early signs can wait for another day, sometimes a week.
meltdown.looks: Suddenly he’s shouting, or crying, or running, and it looks far, far bigger than whatever just happened.
meltdown.an.0: A bath overflowing because the tap was never turned off.
meltdown.other: Frightening, if you’re the one standing nearby. Embarrassing, if it’s in a shop. And people very often feel it must be their fault, and don’t know what to do with their hands.
chain: Input keeps coming, noise and demands and change
The brain’s buffer fills up
When it overflows, control goes
A meltdown is an overflow, and nobody chooses it to get something
meltdown.care_print: Afterwards, a repair and a plan for next time help both people.

dont-know-feeling.say: “I really don’t know yet. Ask me about my body. Am I tired, tense or hungry?”
dont-know-feeling.step: Try simpler questions about the body. “More tired or more annoyed?” “Space or company?” Give it time and come back to it later, or tomorrow.
dont-know-feeling.looks: “How are you feeling about it?” “I don’t know.” And he really does seem stuck, not dodging.
dont-know-feeling.an.0: A radio caught between two stations, all hiss.
dont-know-feeling.other: It’s hard to be on the asking end. You can start to suspect something is being kept from you, when it may simply not have a name yet.
chain: Feelings start as signals in the body
Some people find those signals hard to read
No clear signal, no clear word
“I don’t know” is the honest answer

last-straw.fits: Stress builds up and makes small things feel bigger. The reaction belongs to the whole day.
last-straw.step: Say “I’m nearly full today” early, before the mug. Afterwards, apologise for the size of it, and talk about the mug another time, if it still matters.
last-straw.looks: One mug, left on the side, after a long, long day. And off she goes.
last-straw.an.0: The last drop of rain that makes the gutter overflow.
last-straw.other: Whoever left the mug gets the whole day poured over them. That feels unfair, because it is.
chain: Stress builds up all day
Each thing fills the glass a little more
The mug is the last drop, and what spills is the whole glass

same-food.an.0: A favourite mug. Any mug holds tea; this one is right.
same-food.say: “I eat this because it’s safe and easy for me. It says nothing about your cooking.”
same-food.looks: Cheese sandwich, white bread, every lunchtime, for three years. Anything new is politely declined.
same-food.other: The cook has stood over a hob for an hour, so a polite “no thank you” can feel like the effort being refused. Families worry about health, too, and about every meal out.
chain: Every new food is a small gamble
A known food is a sure thing
Sure things save energy for the rest of the day
same-food.step: Keep a “safe” option on the table next to anything new. Try new food on calm days, one small taste at a time, and no fuss either way.

on-time-means.an.0: A recipe that says “a pinch”, when everyone’s pinch is different.
on-time-means.step: Say which kind of time you mean, such as “Seven sharp, the table is booked” or “Any time after seven.”
on-time-means.other: The one who came at seven sharp sat with the wine going warm and the food going cold, wondering whether they mattered less.
on-time-means.looks: Dinner at seven. Bayo arrives at seven, on the dot, with wine. Shelley arrives at twenty to eight and thinks she’s on time.
chain: “Seven o’clock” gets read through a local rule
In some families it means seven exactly, in others “from seven”
Each of them arrived at the time their rule calls polite

loud-family.looks: Your first dinner at his family’s. Everyone talking at once, at full volume, over each other. To you it sounds exactly like a row.
loud-family.an.0: A Saturday market, where the shouting is how business gets done.
loud-family.other: Someone from a quieter home can sit through a whole dinner without getting a word in, and go home sure everyone was cross. By that family’s standards it was a lovely evening.
chain: Every family has its own volume, and its own rules for whose turn it is
In some homes, talking over each other means everyone’s involved
Loud can mean warm
The noise is their normal, and nobody is fighting
loud-family.step: The quieter person can take short breaks, or ask a direct question to get a turn. The family can stop now and then and ask them in by name.

direct-culture.step: Ask early: “Do you like feedback straight, or with some cushioning?” Then agree a style for the team and write it down somewhere people will see it.
direct-culture.other: The softer speaker can feel attacked. The plainer speaker can feel misled when the soft words turn out to have been hiding a real problem.
direct-culture.looks: One new colleague says “This is wrong” in the meeting. Another says “Maybe we could think about it a bit more,” and also means “This is wrong.”
chain: How directly people give feedback is learned
In some workplaces, plain words show respect
In others, softer words protect the relationship

text-generations.an.0: Handwriting, neat or scrawly. It says nothing about how they feel about you.
text-generations.step: Talk about it once, on a calm day. What does “OK.” mean to each of you? When is a call welcome, and when would a text do?
text-generations.looks: Mum replies “OK.” with a full stop, and her teenager reads pure fury. Meanwhile Grandad has rung, again, about something a text would have covered.
text-generations.other: “OK.” with a full stop reads, to some people, like a door being shut. The writer usually meant nothing of the kind.
chain: Texting habits are learned in a particular time and group
For some, a full stop just ends a sentence; for others it means annoyed
Phoning can mean care to one person and intrusion to another

hungry-tired-snap.looks: Six o’clock. Nothing since a biscuit at eleven. “Have you seen the scissors?” gets a “No” that could cut them.
hungry-tired-snap.an.0: A car running on fumes, jerking at every junction.
hungry-tired-snap.other: The person who asked about the scissors did nothing wrong, and they still got the sharp end. If it happens often enough, they start to tiptoe round you at teatime.
chain: Patience runs on fuel
Hunger and tiredness drain the tank
On an empty tank, small things feel big
The snap is the fuel gauge talking

alone-after-people.looks: The visitors’ car is barely off the drive and he’s already halfway up the stairs. The bedroom door shuts. Quietly, but it shuts.
alone-after-people.an.0: Wringing out a sponge so it can hold water again.
alone-after-people.other: His partner wanted to go over the whole afternoon together, who said what about whose new kitchen. Now she’s on her own with the washing-up, wondering what she did.
chain: Time with people can be lovely and still cost something
The cost has to be paid back
Quiet is how it gets paid
After it, he comes back down, and he’s himself again

long-goodbye.looks: “Right, we’d better be off.” Forty minutes later, everyone’s still on the doorstep with their coats on, and the children are asleep in the car.
long-goodbye.other: For someone whose energy ran out an hour ago, every minute on the doorstep costs. Children may be asleep in the car.
chain: Leaving can feel like the end of the closeness
A slow goodbye winds it down gently
It’s a soft landing for a good evening
long-goodbye.step: Start the goodbye ten minutes earlier than you think you need to. Agree a family signal that means “It’s time. Last bits now.”

unasked-advice.looks: Three in the morning, you’re finally getting the baby down, and your mother-in-law appears in the doorway. “In my day we just let them cry.”
unasked-advice.other: At three in the morning “Have you tried…” sounds a lot like “You’re doing it wrong.”
chain: Advice is how some people show care
They learned things the hard way
Passing it on is trying to spare you that

shutdown.looks: She stops talking and stares at a point somewhere past your shoulder, and questions get nothing back at all.
shutdown.an.0: A computer restarting in safe mode.
shutdown.other: People nearby can feel ignored or frightened, or sure they caused it, so they ask more questions. That usually makes it longer.
chain: Overload builds
The system switches off whatever isn’t essential
Speech is often the first thing to go

info-dump.looks: You asked one question about the 1950s railway timetable. That was twenty minutes ago.
info-dump.an.0: Showing someone round your allotment, bed by bed.
info-dump.other: Twenty minutes into the railway timetable the listener is lost, slightly trapped and far too polite to say either.
chain: The interest is where they feel most themselves
Sharing it is sharing themselves
The detail is the gift
A long explanation is an invitation in
info-dump.step: Start with the five-minute version and ask “Want more?” If you’re listening, “Tell me the best bit” works surprisingly well, and so does “Can we pause there and come back to it?”

boxset.title: Spread Love & Acceptance: The Complete Series
boxset.sub: Books 1–4 and The Logic Behind It
boxset.line: Five books in one Kindle edition: know yourself, steady yourself, understand each other, share the load, and see the logic behind a reaction.
boxset.blurb: The whole Spread Love & Acceptance series in one Kindle edition. Book 1, Know Yourself Kindly, starts with you: where your way of seeing things came from, your wiring, your feelings and your worth. Book 2, Heal and Steady, is for the heavy days of stress, anger, worry, grief and repair. Book 3, Understanding Each Other, looks at how we hear, see and belong to each other. Book 4, Share the Load, makes the unseen work at home visible and offers a fair, kind way to share it. The Logic Behind It, a pocket guide, lays out the reasoning behind thirty-eight everyday reactions that can look odd or rude from outside. Every chapter is also free to read online.
